The insurance hypothesis holds that species differ in their responses to environmental fluctuation, so that communities with more species maintain more stable aggregate productivity as conditions change, which helps preserve consistent levels of biomass production across varying environmental conditions. 

Building on this, functional redundancy, in which several species perform overlapping ecological roles, buffers ecosystem processes against the loss of any single species, and this buffer erodes as species are removed, thereby exposing vital functions to greater risk from further declines in diversity.
